source_text: Ὁ μὲν ἄρα ἀληθῶς καὶ καλῶς πλούσιός ἐστιν ὁ τῶν ἀρετῶν πλούσιος καὶ πάσῃ τύχῃ χρῆσθαι ὁσίως καὶ πιστῶς δυνάμενος, ὁ δὲ νόθος πλούσιος ὁ κατὰ σάρκα πλουτῶν καὶ τὴν ζωὴν εἰς τὴν ἔξω κτῆσιν μετενηνοχὼς τὴν παρερχομένην καὶ φθειρομένην καὶ ἄλλοτε ἄλλου γινομένην καὶ ἐν τῷ τέλει μηδενὸς μηδαμῇ. πάλιν αὖ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ γνήσιος πτωχὸς καὶ νόθος ἄλλος πτωχὸς καὶ ψευδώνυμος. ὃ μὲν κατὰ πνεῦμα πτωχός. τὸ ἴδιον, ὃ δὲ κατὰ κόσμον. τὸ ἀλλότριον. τῷ δὴ κατὰ κόσμον οὐ πτωχῷ καὶ πλουσίῳ κατὰ τὰ πάθη ὁ κατὰ πνεῦμα οὐ πτωχὸς καὶ κατὰ θεὸν πλούσιος ›ἀπόστηθι‹ φησί ›τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ σου κτημάτων ἀλλοτρίων. ἵνα καθαρὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ γενόμενος ἴδῃς τὸν θεόν, ὅπερ καὶ δι᾿ ἑτέρας φωνῆς ἐστιν εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν. καὶ πῶς αὐτῶν ἀποστῇς; πωλήσας. τί οὖν; χρήματα ἀντὶ κτημάτων λάβῃς; ἀντίδοσιν πλούτου πρὸς πλοῦτον ποιησάμενος. ἐξαργυρίσας τὴν φανερὰν οὐσίαν; οὐδαμῶς· ἀλλὰ ἀντὶ τῶν πρότερον ἐνυπαρχόντων τῇ ψυχῇ, ἣν σῶσαι ποθεῖς, ἀντεισαγόμενος ἕτερον πλοῦτον θεοποιὸν καὶ ζωῆς χορηγὸν αἰωνίου, τὰς κατὰ τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ διαθέσεις. ἀνθ᾿ ὧν σοι περιέσται μισθὸς καὶ τιμή. διηνεκὴς σωτηρία καὶ αἰώνιος ἀφθαρσία. οὕτως καλῶς πωλεῖς τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, τὰ πολλὰ καὶ περισσὰ καὶ ἀποκλείοντά σοι τοὺς οὐρανούς. ἀντικαταλλασσόμενος αὐτῶν τὰ σῶσαι δυνάμενα.
thought_title: True and counterfeit wealth and poverty
orientation: Clement is explaining that the rich man's command to sell his possessions refers to the soul's inner possessions, not outward goods.
pass_a_gloss: The one therefore truly and beautifully rich is the one rich in virtues and able to use every fortune holily and faithfully, but the bastard rich person is the one rich according to the flesh and having transferred his life to the outward possession, the one passing away and being corrupted and at different times belonging to different people and in the end belonging to no one in any way. Again in turn according to the same manner there is also a genuine poor person and another bastard poor person and falsely named. The one is poor according to the spirit, which is his own, but the other is poor according to the world, which is alien. To the one then not poor according to the world and rich according to the passions, the one not poor according to the spirit and rich according to God says, 'Stand away from the possessions in your soul, the alien possessions, so that having become pure in heart you may see God, which is also through another voice to enter into the kingdom of heaven. And how may you stand away from them? By selling. What then? That you may take money in exchange for possessions? Having made an exchange of wealth for wealth, having turned the visible substance into silver? By no means; but instead of the things formerly existing in the soul, which you long to save, bringing in another wealth that makes divine and supplies eternal life, the dispositions according to the commandment of God. In exchange for which there will remain for you a reward and honor, continuous salvation and eternal incorruption. Thus beautifully you sell your existing things, the many and superfluous things that shut off the heavens to you, exchanging for them the things able to save.

choices.why: Clement contrasts genuine and counterfeit wealth; 'bastard' preserves the strong pejorative sense of illegitimate or spurious, matching his rhetorical contrast with 'genuine'.
The phrase sets up the flesh/spirit contrast that structures the whole passage; 'according to the flesh' keeps the Pauline idiom.
The imperative is addressed to the soul's inner possessions; 'stand away' preserves the spatial force of the verb and its command form.
The verb is a vivid coinage meaning to convert into silver money; the literal rendering keeps Clement's rhetorical question about whether selling means cashing out.
The adjective describes the new wealth as deifying; the literal rendering preserves the startling force of the word.

choices.english: that shut off the heavens to you
choices.why: The participle describes the superfluous possessions as actively closing heaven; the literal rendering keeps the verb's force and the dative of disadvantage.

bible_refs.note: καθαρὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ γενόμενος ἴδῃς τὸν θεόν

pass_b_english: So the truly and rightly rich person is the one rich in virtues, able to use every circumstance in a holy and faithful way. The false rich person is the one rich according to the flesh, who has transferred his life to outward possessions that pass away and decay, that belong now to one person and now to another, and in the end to no one at all. In the same way again, there is a genuine poor person and another poor person who is bastard and falsely named. The one is poor according to the spirit, which is his own; the other is poor according to the world, which is alien to him. He says to the one who is not poor according to the world but rich in the passions, and to the one who is not poor according to the spirit but rich according to God: “Stand away from the alien possessions that dwell in your soul, so that, becoming pure in heart, you may see God”—which is the same thing, in another phrase, as entering the kingdom of heaven. And how will you stand away from them? By selling them. What then? Will you take money in exchange for possessions, making an exchange of wealth for wealth, having turned your visible substance into silver? Not at all. Instead, in place of the things that formerly dwelt in the soul you long to save, you bring in another wealth that makes divine and supplies eternal life: the dispositions that follow the commandment of God. In return for these you will have a reward and honor: unceasing salvation and eternal incorruption. In this way you sell your possessions well—the many and superfluous ones that shut off the heavens to you—exchanging them in return for the things that are able to save.

problems.quote: The bastard rich person is the one rich according to the flesh, who has transferred his life to outward possessions that pass away and decay, that belong now to one person and now to another, and in the end to no one at all.
problems.source_quote: ὁ δὲ νόθος πλούσιος ὁ κατὰ σάρκα πλουτῶν καὶ τὴν ζωὴν εἰς τὴν ἔξω κτῆσιν μετενηνοχὼς τὴν παρερχομένην καὶ φθειρομένην καὶ ἄλλοτε ἄλλου γινομένην καὶ ἐν τῷ τέλει μηδενὸς μηδαμῇ.
problems.why: "νόθος" means false/spurious, not "bastard"; the term violates the glossary and adds a pejorative sense.
problems.fix: The false rich person is the one rich according to the flesh, who has transferred his life to outward possessions that pass away and decay, that belong now to one person and now to another, and in the end to no one at all.

edits.old: The bastard rich person is the one rich according to the flesh
edits.new: The false rich person is the one rich according to the flesh

fixed: Changed 'bastard rich person' to 'false rich person' because νόθος here means spurious/false, not illegitimate, and the glossary bans pejorative terms.

problems.quote: the one who is not poor according to the world but rich in the passions, the one who is not poor according to the spirit but rich according to God says:
problems.source_quote: τῷ δὴ κατὰ κόσμον οὐ πτωχῷ ... ἀποστῆθι φησί
problems.why: Greek says the teacher says to the addressed persons; English makes it sound like the addressed person is speaking.
problems.fix: He says to the one who is not poor according to the world but rich in the passions, and to the one who is not poor according to the spirit but rich according to God: “Stand away …”
problems.ruling: τῷ δὴ κατὰ κόσμον οὐ πτωχῷ is dative: 'says TO the one...'; English 'the one...says' reverses speaker and addressee.

edits.old: To the one who is not poor according to the world but rich in the passions, the one who is not poor according to the spirit but rich according to God says:
edits.new: He says to the one who is not poor according to the world but rich in the passions, and to the one who is not poor according to the spirit but rich according to God:

fixed: Agency: Greek has φησί with the speaker (the one rich according to God) addressing the two types of persons; English made the addressed persons the subject of 'says'. Changed to 'He says to...' to restore the speaker as the subject.

problems.why: Same concept phrased differently; reader may miss the equivalence.
problems.fix: Use 'poor in spirit' consistently with a note on first variation.

problems.quote: another poor person who is bastard and falsely named
problems.why: 'Bastard' as an adjective is archaic and jarring; the context needs 'illegitimate' or 'spurious.'

edits.old: another poor person who is bastard and falsely named
edits.new: another poor person who is spurious and falsely named

fixed: Glossary problem: 'poor in spirit' is not in the English; the English uses 'poor according to the spirit,' which is a literal rendering of κατὰ πνεῦμα πτωχός and is not a mistranslation. No edit made.
Mistranslation: 'bastard' is a literal rendering of νόθος and is not a mistranslation, but it is archaic and jarring; changed to 'spurious' to fit modern literary English.

last_rejected.why: Greek ψευδώνυμος means ‘falsely named’; ‘bastard’ adds an unrelated sense.
last_rejected.ruling: νόθος means 'bastard/illegitimate'; pairing with ψευδώνυμος ('falsely named') is accurate, not an added sense.
